blocks.text: Count the sachet water brands on one street in Lagos, then count the cement companies in the whole of Nigeria. Both markets are competitive, but in completely different ways: hundreds of tiny water producers each with a loyal handful of customers, and a mere handful of cement giants each watching the others like hawks. Real markets live between the extremes of perfect competition and pure monopoly.

blocks.markdown: **Imperfect competition** is the name given to every market structure that is neither perfectly competitive nor a pure monopoly. The two most important are **monopolistic competition** and **oligopoly**. Both give the firm some power over its own price, which is why the demand curve facing the individual firm slopes downward in each case.

blocks.title: Monopolistic competition
blocks.text: A market with a large number of sellers offering closely related but differentiated products, with free entry into and exit from the industry. Each firm holds a small monopoly over its own brand, so it faces a downward-sloping but highly elastic demand curve.

items: **Many sellers and many buyers**, as in perfect competition.
**Product differentiation** — goods differ in brand, packaging, quality, after-sales service or location, even though they serve the same need.
**Free entry and exit**, so only normal profit survives in the long run.
**Heavy advertising and sales promotion**, because differentiation must be advertised to be believed.
**Some price control** — a firm can raise price a little without losing all its customers, since some buyers are loyal to the brand.
**Highly elastic firm demand curve**, because close substitutes are everywhere.
**Examples in Nigeria**: sachet water, provision shops, tailoring, restaurants, hair salons, bread bakeries, soap and detergent.

blocks.markdown:
### Oligopoly

**Oligopoly** is a market dominated by a **few large sellers**, each supplying a significant share of total output. When there are only two firms the market is called a **duopoly**.

The defining feature is **interdependence**. Because each firm is large, any change it makes to price or output is felt by its rivals, who will react. So every firm must guess how its rivals will respond before it acts — something no firm in the other three structures needs to do.

This produces two familiar consequences:

- **Price rigidity.** Prices tend to stay unchanged for long periods. A firm that cuts price expects rivals to follow, so it gains little and everyone earns less; a firm that raises price expects rivals to hold steady, so it loses customers. The safest move is not to move at all. This is often illustrated by the **kinked demand curve**.
- **Non-price competition.** Since price changes are risky, firms compete through advertising, branding, free gifts, promotions, warranties, packaging and product improvement instead.

items: **Few firms**, each with a large market share, so entry barriers exist but are not absolute.
**Interdependence** in decision making — the central feature.
**Products may be identical** (petrol, cement) **or differentiated** (cars, mobile networks, beer).
**Price rigidity** and a tendency towards non-price competition.
**Possibility of collusion** — firms may secretly agree on price or output, or form a **cartel** to act as a single monopolist. OPEC, of which Nigeria is a member, is the best-known cartel.
**Price leadership** — one dominant firm sets the price and the others follow.
**Examples in Nigeria**: cement, telecommunications, banking, brewing, petroleum marketing, flour milling.

blocks.title: Identifying a market structure from a description
blocks.prompt: In a Nigerian city, eleven companies bottle and sell soft drinks. The four largest supply about 85 per cent of the market, each brand has its own flavour and bottle shape, all four advertise on television constantly, and prices have not changed in two years even though costs have risen. Which market structure is this, and what evidence supports your answer?

steps.text: Count the effective sellers. Although eleven firms exist, four supply 85 per cent of output, so the market is dominated by a few large firms. That points away from monopolistic competition, which requires many firms of comparable size.
There is more than one seller, so it cannot be a monopoly. The products are branded and differentiated, so it cannot be perfect competition either.
Test the diagnostic features of oligopoly. Heavy television advertising is non-price competition, the classic oligopolistic response to the risk of price cutting.
Prices unchanged for two years despite rising costs is price rigidity — the strongest single clue. Each firm fears that a price rise will be unmatched and a price cut will be followed.
Both clues follow from interdependence: each of the four firms is large enough that its rivals must react to whatever it does.

blocks.answer: Oligopoly. The evidence is domination by a few large firms, differentiated branded products, heavy non-price competition through advertising, and price rigidity arising from interdependence

blocks.title: The number of firms alone will not identify the structure
blocks.text: Both perfect and monopolistic competition have many firms; the difference is whether the product is homogeneous or differentiated. Both monopoly and oligopoly can earn long-run abnormal profit; the difference is one seller against a few. Always name **two** distinguishing features, not one, when an examiner asks you to classify a market.

points: Imperfect competition covers all structures between perfect competition and pure monopoly.
Monopolistic competition has many sellers, differentiated products, free entry, heavy advertising and only normal profit in the long run.
Each firm in monopolistic competition faces a downward-sloping but highly elastic demand curve, giving it slight control over price.
Oligopoly is domination by a few large interdependent firms, so each must anticipate its rivals' reactions.
Interdependence produces price rigidity, illustrated by the kinked demand curve, and shifts competition towards advertising and branding.
Oligopolists may collude or form a cartel, such as OPEC, to behave like a single monopolist.
The four structures are best compared on number of firms, nature of the product, ease of entry, control over price and long-run profit.
